extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, members of learned societies, and educated readers interested in 18th-century natural philosophy and practical electrical/earth science
extracted.subtask_description: 18th-century essays/letters (Benjamin Franklin) on magnetism, the origin of coal, causes and classifications of earthquakes, theories of light and heat, and practical methods for protecting buildings and persons from lightning. Mixes theoretical conjectures with observational and experimental guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider external causes for Earth's magnetism
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether the earth received its magnetism from an external cause rather than from iron ore originally present (e.g., a magnetic power pervading systems or imparted by passing bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin asks whether iron ore existed immediately at formation or was produced gradually, whether earth's magnetism might have been obtained from an external magnetic power (perhaps universal) and whether a passing large comet of greater magnetic power might have changed the poles, deranged the surface, and produced deluges and other global effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow hypothesis of universal/subsystem magnetism
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility that a magnetic power exists throughout a system (or systems) so compasses might work across starry regions, and that such uniform magnetism could stabilize diurnal revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought experiments about voyages in starry regions; consider uniform direction and dynamical effects (keeping planetary axis steady) when evaluating planetary magnetism hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pole-shift hypothesis for geological and climatic anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion that changes of magnetic poles (e.g., by influence of a stronger magnet) could have changed planetary poles and thereby explain occurrences such as tropical shells in polar regions and the deluge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin reasons that pole change would cause sea level shifts (e.g., ~15 miles if poles moved to equator) and could relocate climatic zones; use pole-shift as a parsimonious account for large-scale paleoclimatic evidence and floodwater disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal-fluid (dense) globe hypothesis to explain surface wrecking
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose that the earth's internal mass may be a very dense fluid supporting a brittle shell; movement of that internal fluid could alter shell form, burst it, and raise parts of the surface (analogous to changing an egg's internal fluid orientation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the egg analogy: if internal substance is fluid and dense, shifts in the internal fluid or waves can fracture the shell and produce mountain ridges and rearranged strata; assess stratal disarrangements in light of internal fluid behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal ocean wave mechanism for earthquakes and rumbling sound
rubrics_metrics.description: A wave in the supposed internal dense fluid may raise and break the surface shell in places, causing earthquakes; the wave's progression explains rumbling heard first at a distance and increasing toward the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this mechanism to observed seismic phenomena such as the long-traced rumbling reported in South America (from north of Lima to Buenos Ayres) and the gradation of noise intensity as a wave approaches and passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seacoal (coal) vegetable origin and near-surface formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Seacoal is of vegetable origin and was formed near the surface; later convulsions buried it under strata and brought it deeper, though mining can encounter veins descending under the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support this with field evidence such as leaf and fern impressions in slate above coal seams (e.g., Whitehaven coalmine) and observations of gradual descent of seams below sea level; use such evidence when evaluating coal origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earthquake cause: collapse/sinking from dissolved or worn-away supports
rubrics_metrics.description: The earth may shake when the roots or basis of a large mass are dissolved or worn away by an underlying fluid, causing that mass to sink and tremble adjacent parts, produce noise, and cause inundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider local geological undermining (dissolution, subrosion) as a causal explanation for tremors, noises, and sudden subsidence of tracts of land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earthquake cause: subterranean waters overflowing or being heated
rubrics_metrics.description: Subterranean waters may overflow, cut new courses, or be heated by subterranean fires, emitting fumes and blasts that act either on the water or directly on the earth to produce strong shocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the combined effects of water movement and heating (rarefaction, vapour production) to explain eruptions of water, thermal anomalies in springs after quakes, and violent ground motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earthquake cause: pent-up air or vapours (aura) expanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Air as a collection of vapours, if pent in narrow subterranean cavities and heated, expands and exerts force to escape, producing shaking; different positions and quantities of imprisoned aura lead to different earthquake species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish earthquake types by the configuration and confinement of subterranean air: degree of confinement, heat, and quantity determine violence and character of the tremor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earthquake cause: subterranean fire igniting inflammable vapours (pyrites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire under the ground (either producing or igniting inflammable vapours from pyrites and sulphurous matter) can burst into larger compass, pressing on adjoining parts and causing shocks and volcanoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the similarity in sulphurous smell found with lightning burns and with waters/gases after quakes; consider pyritic sulphur as a key agent producing inflammable vapours contributing to subterranean explosions and volcanic activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between pyrites/sulphur abundance and earthquake frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Regions abundant in pyrites, sulphur, and nitre (e.g., Italy, Mediterranean) suffer more frequent and severe earthquakes than places with less pyrites (e.g., England).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mineralogical surveys (presence of pyrites/sulphur/nitre) and regional geology (cavernous, mountainous strata) to assess earthquake hazard and account for interregional differences in seismicity and thunder/lightning characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dr. Woodward's subterranean-heat-and-water elevation theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Subterranean heat continually elevates water from the abyss for rain and springs; if this heat is diverted by obstructions, it preternaturally assembles, rarefies water, causes intumescence and violent commotions, tearing chasms and sometimes forcing out strata and water to form lakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model explains cracking, chasms, eruptions, and hot waters thrown up; severity is modulated by regional geology (mountainous, cavernous, composition of strata) and by presence of vents (volcanoes) that act as discharge spiracles or diverticula; theorize that where vents exist, shocks may be relieved and diminished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of strata composition and structure in earthquake severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries with stony or marble strata oppose subterranean efforts more strongly and are thus more furiously shattered in earthquakes than regions of gravel and sand which give way more easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess local stratigraphy when estimating earthquake damage patterns: stronger, rigid strata produce greater destructive shock and fracturing; looser sediments attenuate the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-compression/deep-heat (Amontons) hypothesis for earthquakes
rubrics_metrics.description: At great depths air is highly compressed and heavy; moderate heat at such depths may increase the spring of the air dramatically, so that deep heat could exert violent effects capable of breaking and overturning solid strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical experiments on the weight and spring of air and scaling arguments (compression depth comparisons) to evaluate plausibility of deep-air expansion as a seismic driver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial production of earthquakes demonstrates chemical mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A buried mixture of iron filings and sulphur (mixed with a little water to form a semi-wet mass) produces violent tremors, cracks, smoke, and fire and flame within hours, illustrating how subterranean chemical reactions can mimic natural earthquakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin gives an explicit recipe (twenty pounds iron filings + twenty pounds sulphur, mixed with water, buried 3–4 feet) as an experimental demonstration; use caution — this is an illustration of mechanism rather than a safety recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earthquake definition and classical classification
rubrics_metrics.description: An earthquake is a vehement shake or agitation of some considerable place from natural causes, attended with huge noise like thunder and often with eruptions of water, fire, smoke, or winds; classical kinds include tremour (horizontal vibration) and pulsation (perpendicular), with other taxonomies (Agricola, Albertus Magnus) expanding types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify seismic motions as tremour (alternating horizontal), pulsation (up/down), inclination (vibrates to meet), and trembling (totters every way); use observational descriptors (bells ringing, people thrown off feet) to categorize events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of light and heat as vibration of a subtile fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal space may be filled with a subtile fluid whose motion or vibration is called light; this same fluid may be that which when entering solids dilutes them and constitutes heat/fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat light as continuous vibrational motion transmitted through a subtile medium; consider heat as the fluid's presence in organized bodies (natural heat), excess as fever, and violent external influx as burning. Use analogies of vapour separation, absorption, and conservation of this fluid to explain heating and combustion phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation-separation view of fire/heat
rubrics_metrics.description: If fire is an original element or kind of matter, its quantity is fixed in the universe; humans cannot create or annihilate it, only separate it from bodies (e.g., burning wood leaves fire in lime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret combustion, heating, and natural animal heat as processes of separating and localizing the subtile fire fluid; use this view when reasoning about sources and sinks of heat in natural processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning is the same as electric matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments on electricity and lightning show that lightning is the same as the electric matter (the subtle fluid) — properties observed in small electrical experiments are found in lightning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply results from small-scale electrical experiments to understand atmospheric lightning; treat electric phenomena and lightning as manifestations of the same fluid and laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of electric fluid during discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: When one body has more of the electric fluid than another it will communicate to the other until proportions equalize; if communication is through air without a conductor, bright light (spark) and sound occur; if via a conductor, discharge may be without light or sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the distinction between discharge through air (spark + snap) and discharge via conductor (silent, fluid passing within conductor) to predict observational differences and hazards during charged-cloud events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Striking distance concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance at which a charged body will suddenly discharge through the air into another body depends on fluid quantity, dimensions and shape of bodies, and the state of the intervening air; this is called the 'striking distance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing lightning risk, consider how much charge, geometry of objects, and atmospheric conditions determine whether a discharge will leap through the air or seek a conductor; objects within striking distance can be hit even if not the tallest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conductivity rules: good and poor conductors
rubrics_metrics.description: All metals and water are good conductors. Some building materials (wood, etc.) can conduct if containing water; perfectly dry wood, glass, wax, silk, wool, hair, feathers are non-conductors (resist passage of fluid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or analyzing protection, rely on metal and water paths for conduction to earth; beware that otherwise-insulating materials become conductive when wet, and that non-conductors concentrate rather than conduct the electric fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conductor adequacy: size and sufficiency matters
rubrics_metrics.description: If a conductor is good and of sufficient bigness the electric fluid passes through it without hurting it; if not, the conductor is damaged or destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide conductors of adequate cross-section and continuity to safely conduct large discharges; undersized or intermittent conductors can be burned or damaged during a strike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tall trees and lofty buildings as hazardous conductors when not adequately metallic
rubrics_metrics.description: Tall trees and lofty buildings sometimes become conductors between clouds and earth; when they are not good conductors they often suffer damage (trees splintered, buildings damaged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that height increases exposure; ensure tall structures have proper metallic conductors to ground to avoid destructive internal or wall discharges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metal roofing and continuous metal spouts to ground protect buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings with roofs covered with lead or other metal and with metal spouts continued from the roof into the ground to carry off water are never hurt by lightning, because the fluid passes through the metals and not through the walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuous metallic roofing and down-conductors tied to earth to provide a preferred pathway for lightning to ground; continuity from roof to earth is essential to prevent the fluid from traversing walls or other structural elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearby conductors and internal conductive elements create alternate discharge paths
rubrics_metrics.description: When a building is within striking distance of a charged cloud the fluid may pass in the walls and quit them only when finding better conductors near (metal rods, bolts, hinges, gilding, silvering on mirrors, bell wires, animal bodies containing watery fluids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect and mitigate conductive attachments and fixtures (metal fasteners, decorative gilding, bell wiring) which can provide undesired discharge paths; prefer robust, dedicated conductors to avoid partial wall conduction and secondary damage to occupants or contents.
